source.authors: Brandon A. Güell, Karen M. Warkentin
source.title: When and where to hatch? Red-eyed treefrog embryos use light cues in two contexts

method: behavioural: direction of hatching out of a tube with one end illuminated (half-dark cup), single embryos
conditions: Wild-collected egg masses (0-3 days old, Experimental Pond, Gamboa, Panama); individual 3-day-old eggs placed in a clear tube in the wall of a half-dark cup, one side lit and one dark, alternating the side of insertion (alternated, not randomised); hatching phototaxis tested at 4 days of age between 12:00 and 17:00; 92 embryos from 39 clutches tested in half-dark cups, 85 analysed (reason for the 7 exclusions not read); overall 59 of 85 hatched toward the light (69.4%), chi-square against equal proportions p < 0.001 (Results); no difference between the two sets of illuminated trials (higher and lower illumination, LED lights 10 cm or 15-20 cm above the cups); light intensity was not measured in this experiment (authors' statement); embryos were flooded to induce hatching (per abstract wording, procedure not read). A separate timing experiment in the same paper (photoperiod, continuous light, continuous dark) is not used here.
value: most tested embryos hatched toward the light (59 of 85 in the Results; illumination not measured)
quote: Most embryos hatched toward the light, suggesting they use light as a directional cue.
note: Embryos have eyes at this stage only as developing structures; the paper does not say which photoreceptors mediate the response, so the trait key sense_light_nonvisual is a judgement for a light cue used by an embryo (owner to confirm, or move to behaviour_vision). Family Phyllomedusidae follows main's Thomas et al. 2022 rows for this species (another main row says Hylidae); name Agalychnis callidryas accepted in GBIF per docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv. source.authors: Cutter J. Barrus, Kaiyuan Zheng, Britney A. Bender, Charlotte A. Fraley, Bradley P. Roth, Sophia M. Glennie, Rowyn P. Birdsley, Kara G. Pratt
source.title: Individual Xenopus Tadpoles Display Distinct and Consistent Visual Preferences

method: behavioural: single tadpoles tested for 15 min in a dish with one quadrant (25%) shown a test stimulus against the other 75%, retested the next day
conditions: Laboratory-bred tadpoles from in-house matings of wild-type X. laevis; developmental stages 48-49; stimuli displayed on a back-lit monitor and defined by Lab colour values (white L = 100, dark L = 0, green L = 75, a = -75, b = 75), light intensity not reported; each tadpole tested 15 min on one test and retested about 24 h later on the same test; light v dark n = 19, green v light n = 23 (two outliers excluded from the statistics); preference index scores ranged from 0.15 to 0.94 (light v dark) and 0.11 to 1.0 (green v light); the Results give no group-level test statistic for baseline preference (the abstract text 'most tadpoles preferred light' and 'majority preferred green over light' is not tested in the passages read); inter-clutch variability statistically nonsignificant; drug experiments (pCPA, fluoxetine) not used here; statistics for the stability of individual preferences not read.
value: preferences varied across tadpoles and were stable within individuals over time (green v light and light v dark tests)
quote: While preferences varied across tadpoles, preferences displayed within individuals were stable over time (i.e., consistent).
note: The abstract also reports that some tadpoles strongly preferred green over light while others preferred light over green (sentence over 40 words, not quoted). Sentence read whole in the page tool's output. Family and order from main (canon-2 rows for Xenopus laevis). Licence: page metadata CC BY 3.0; Crossref CC BY 4.0, content-version vor. Printed year 2026 (Crossref issued 2026-09-01).

source.authors: Seiya Tsujiuchi, Elena Sivan-Loukianova, Daniel F. Eberl, Yasuo Kitagawa, Tatsuhiko Kadowaki
source.title: Dynamic Range Compression in the Honey Bee Auditory System toward Waggle Dance Sounds

method: electrophysiology: JO sound-evoked potentials from the antennal nerve against laser-vibrometer-measured flagellar tip displacement
conditions: Extracellular sound-evoked potentials (SEPs) recorded from the antennal nerve with the flagellar tip displacement measured by laser Doppler vibrometer (CLV-700) and the air particle velocity by a near-field probe (Microflown), i.e. measured stimuli. Bees: known-age bees from combs of a hive (newly emerged bees marked and returned to the hive) plus pollen foragers of unknown age; wild/hive origin of the colony not otherwise stated. Recordings for each stimulus and age taken from at least 5 animals (Methods). Control: SEPs were no longer detectable after pedicel lesion, so they are attributable to the Johnston's organ (JO). JO responses were lower in newly eclosed (0-day) bees than in 21-day-old foragers; which age group the 20 nm threshold in Fig. 6D comes from is not stated in the passages read. Responses saturate at flagellar tip displacement above 200 nm at 265 Hz (Fig. 6 legend). No temperature reported; statistics for the threshold not read.
value: minimum JO response detected at 20 nm flagellar tip displacement (60 nm air particle displacement)
quote: The minimum response of JO neurons can be detected by 20 nm displacement of the flagellar tip (achieved by 60 nm air particle displacement, [Fig. 6D]).
note: Johnston's organ (antennal) detection of near-field particle displacement, not far-field pressure hearing. The abstract says the flagellum 'is a sensitive movement detector responding to 20 nm tip displacement, which is comparable to female mosquito'. Sentence returned by the page tool in two abutting pieces in one response (said in pieces). Family and order from main (Apis mellifera rows are Apidae, Hymenoptera); not printed in the passages read. source.title: Hyperacute Directional Hearing and Phonotactic Steering in the Cricket (Gryllus bimaculatus deGeer)

method: behavioural: open-loop trackball steering of walking females to a computer-generated calling song played from frontal angles
conditions: Laboratory-reared females (reared individually from the last instar in the Cambridge colony); 15 phonotactically active females, each tested 3 times on consecutive days, at frontal angles up to 30 degrees either side with 0 degrees as each animal's reference; a second group of 15 animals had stimulation angles (0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 20 degrees) randomly varied in order and direction to control for order effects; calling-song model with a 4.8 kHz carrier calibrated with a 1/4-inch free-field microphone at the cricket's position and adjusted to 75 dB SPL (measured stimulus); steering response to 1 degree differed from the response to 0 degrees (t-test, p = 0.01); the steering response of all tested animals was significantly directed to the side of stimulation (Results); at 30 degrees the relative steering response was 186% (25.3 cm/min). Only the calling-song carrier tested; no sham or silent control beyond the 0 degree reference was described.
value: females walked towards the sound source at angles of sound incidence between 1 and 6 degrees
quote: Moreover, for angles of sound incidence between 1° and 6° the females precisely walked towards the sound source.
note: Directional hearing and steering rather than a detection threshold. Family and order from main (Gryllus bimaculatus rows: Gryllidae, Orthoptera). source.title: Hyperacute Directional Hearing and Phonotactic Steering in the Cricket (Gryllus bimaculatus deGeer)

method: laser vibrometry of tympanic membrane oscillations to sound from 30 degrees azimuth (binaural response difference)
conditions: Laboratory-reared Gryllus bimaculatus females (Cambridge colony); calling-song stimulus with a 4.8 kHz carrier at 75 dB SPL calibrated with a free-field microphone at the animal's position (measured); 30 degrees is the largest angle tested; number of animals used for the vibrometry not read; the same paper's behavioural experiment used 15 females tested on 3 consecutive days (see companion record).
quote: For tympanic membrane oscillations the binaural response difference was 12.9±2.7 dB at 30°.
note: Mean plus or minus value as printed (presumably SD or SEM, not stated in the passage read).
